name: King Fahd International Airport
before:
The airport for Dammam and for the whole Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, 31 km north west of the city. It is third in the kingdom by passenger numbers, carrying more than 10 million a year across 37 airlines, and it is the hub for Flynas and Flyadeal.

There are three terminal buildings but a client will only ever use one of them. The Passenger Terminal handles all scheduled traffic. The Aramco Terminal is for Saudi Aramco staff flying to Yanbu, Tanajib and Shaybah, and the Royal Terminal is reserved for the royal family.

Dubai is by far the busiest route, with 70 flights a week, about ten a day.

The airport is newer than its size suggests. It was built as a United States airbase and used mainly during the Gulf War, only opening to commercial traffic in November 1999, replacing Dhahran International which is now King Abdulaziz Air Base. Two runways serve it, each 4 km long.
after:
The airport for Dammam and the whole of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, 31 km north west of the city. One of the kingdom's four main airports, it handles more than 10 million passengers a year and is a hub for Flynas.

All scheduled flights use the one passenger terminal.

It opened to commercial flights in 1999, replacing Dhahran International, which is now King Abdulaziz Air Base. There are two runways, each 4 km long.

FCDO advice against travel in Saudi Arabia covers only the Yemen border area and the cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait. The FCDO also reports Houthi missile and drone attacks on cities and airports across the kingdom since 13 July 2026, and tells British nationals in the Middle East to be prepared for flight cancellations and periodic airspace closures.

claims.note: Was 'third in the kingdom by passenger numbers'. Wikipedia and Airport Technology (undated) both say third, but no source within 12 months ranks it: GACA's and Matarat's sites reset the connection. Arab News (14 December 2025) groups it with Riyadh, Jeddah and Madinah as the four main airports.

claims.claim: more than 10 million passengers a year
claims.inAfter: it handles more than 10 million passengers a year
claims.note: The operator's open data (monthly passengers by route, international and domestic) sums to 12,244,306 passengers for 2024 and 10,965,574 for January to October 2025; 16 cells marked '-' were read as zero. Wikipedia's own statistics section says 'around 9.7 million', which the operator's figures overtake. The text keeps the conservative 'more than 10 million' rather than a summed figure.

claims.note: Arab News (9 June 2025) names Dammam among Flynas's four main hubs. That is 15 months old, so two newer items back it: Arab News (22 July 2026) has Flynas with six Saudi operating bases, and the operator's current home page announces new Flynas flights from the airport to Turaif. Flynas's own site refuses the fetchers (403).

claims.claim: third in the kingdom by passengers; 37 airlines; hub for Flyadeal
claims.wasBefore: It is third in the kingdom by passenger numbers, carrying more than 10 million a year across 37 airlines, and it is the hub for Flynas and Flyadeal.
claims.why: Passengers and the Flynas hub are kept above. The rank is softened (no source within 12 months). The count of 37 airlines has only Wikipedia; the operator's directory could not be counted. Flyadeal's hub has only Wikipedia; its own site refuses the fetchers and the Arab News reports saved do not name its bases.

claims.claim: three terminal buildings, a client uses one
claims.wasBefore: There are three terminal buildings but a client will only ever use one of them.
claims.why: Reworded to what the sources support now (see the passenger terminal claim).

claims.claim: Passenger Terminal handles all scheduled traffic
claims.wasBefore: The Passenger Terminal handles all scheduled traffic.

claims.claim: Aramco Terminal for staff to Yanbu, Tanajib and Shaybah; Royal Terminal for the royal family
claims.wasBefore: The Aramco Terminal is for Saudi Aramco staff flying to Yanbu, Tanajib and Shaybah, and the Royal Terminal is reserved for the royal family.
claims.why: The Aramco Terminal has only Wikipedia. The Royal Terminal is also in Airport Technology (31 July 2023), but that page's own fact box counts two terminals where Wikipedia has three, and a client never uses it.

claims.claim: Dubai is by far the busiest route, 70 flights a week
claims.wasBefore: Dubai is by far the busiest route, with 70 flights a week, about ten a day.
claims.why: Contradicted by the operator's open data. In 2024 Jeddah (2,303,525 passengers) and Riyadh (1,590,310) were far busier than Dubai (811,184), and in January to October 2025 Cairo (732,819) was ahead of Dubai (699,673) too. Dubai had 2,828 departures in 2024, about 54 a week.

claims.claim: newer than its size suggests
claims.wasBefore: The airport is newer than its size suggests.
claims.why: A judgement resting on the airport's land area, which the new text does not give.

claims.claim: built as a US airbase, used mainly in the Gulf War
claims.wasBefore: It was built as a United States airbase and used mainly during the Gulf War
claims.why: Misleading and single-source. Wikipedia says it was built under the Saudi government's airports programme and that US-led coalition forces used it in early 1991; Airport Technology says Bechtel built it for the Saudi Ministry of Defense and Aviation. No second source for the 1991 use could be saved.

claims.claim: opened November 1999 (old wording)
claims.wasBefore: only opening to commercial traffic in November 1999, replacing Dhahran International which is now King Abdulaziz Air Base
claims.why: Month disputed (Wikipedia November, Airport Technology October); reworded with the year only. The Dhahran fact is kept.

claims.claim: two runways, 4 km (old wording)
claims.wasBefore: Two runways serve it, each 4 km long.

reviewed.what: FCDO paragraph made precise (Abha and Khamis Mushait) and the Houthi attacks added, both from the FCDO page.
